passage: By the cowshed in their village, Yash, four, pretended to be a bird. He flapped his arms, ran round the haystack and made a beak with his fingers. His grandmother Aadhya, shelling peas, asked, "Are you a crow or a parrot?" He looked at her, shy, and kept flapping. She guessed. "A parrot! Green wings." He grinned. Then he cupped his hands to his mouth and made a drinking gesture. "You want water, little bird?" Yash nodded and she brought a cup.

qa.q: What did Yash pretend to be by the cowshed?
qa.a: He pretended to be a bird.

qa.q: What does Yash's grin and his switching to a drinking gesture suggest he was thinking?
qa.a: He seems happy that his grandmother understood his pretend play, and used mime for the water because words felt hard for him with shyness. He might also simply have been thirsty.

qa.q: What could Aadhya do to help Yash use words when he's ready?
qa.a: She can keep guessing playfully and sometimes offer a word for what he mimed, without pressing him to speak.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel as she guesses what Yash is miming?
qa.a: She may feel amused and close to him, enjoying the game while working out what he needs.

grounding: A preschooler mimes being a bird and drinking, and a shy child relies on the adult to guess.

passage: On a beach in Lagos, Emeka, five, held his hands like a steering wheel and made engine noises. His friend Wei, not sure what Emeka was doing, stared at him. Emeka waved a hand for Wei to come closer, turned an imaginary wheel and honked with the flat of his hand. "Oh! You're driving!" said Wei. Emeka nodded and pointed at the empty sand beside him. Wei climbed into the invisible car. They drove past the ice-cream stall and stopped for an imaginary fuel fill-up.

qa.q: What did Emeka use his hands to be?
qa.a: He held his hands like a steering wheel.

qa.q: What did Emeka seem to want when he pointed at the empty sand?
qa.a: He wanted Wei to join him in the pretend car, and he used gestures because his first try wasn't understood. He might also have wanted to show off his idea.

qa.q: How could Wei help a friend whose mime Wei doesn't understand at first?
qa.a: Wei can keep watching and guess, as before, and ask questions like "Are you driving?"

qa.q: How might Wei have felt when he first couldn't work out the mime?
qa.a: Wei may have felt puzzled, and then pleased and included once the mime made sense.

grounding: A preschooler mimes driving and the friend has to guess, showing imagination and the limits of gesture without words.

passage: In the clinic waiting room, Chinmay held his arm and wouldn't talk. Nurse Indu knelt. “Can you show me what happened?” Chinmay stood up, pretended to hold two chains, swung his legs forward, then let go of the chains and flopped onto his side. “You fell off a swing?” He nodded. “And where does it hurt?” He mimed hitting the ground with his elbow, then pointed at it. “Thank you,” said Indu. “That was very clear.” Chinmay sat down, a little less pale.

qa.q: How did Chinmay show he fell?
qa.a: He pretended to hold two chains, swung his legs forward, then let go and flopped onto his side.

qa.q: Why might Chinmay have mimed instead of talking?
qa.a: He was probably shy with the nurse and scared about his sore arm, so miming felt easier than finding words.

qa.q: What did Indu do that helped Chinmay explain?
qa.a: She asked him to show her, guessed out loud, and thanked him, so he could explain without words.

qa.q: How might Indu feel when the mime makes things clear?
qa.a: She likely feels relieved to know how he got hurt, which helps her decide what to check.

grounding: A shy preschooler at a clinic uses mime to explain how he got hurt when words fail.

passage: I'm Kavitha, Aditi's big sister. Today Aditi set her dolls in a row and poured them tea from an empty hand, lifting her little finger like Nani does. Then she pretended to drive them to the market, turning a steering wheel that wasn't there and going “Pom pom!” Later she ran to Nani, flapping her arms and pointing at the window. Nani said, “A crow?” Aditi shook her head and flapped harder. Nani tried, “A big bird?” Aditi shouted, “Peacock!” We all ran to see it.

qa.q: What did Aditi pretend to drive?
qa.a: She pretended to drive her dolls to the market, turning a steering wheel that wasn't there.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she flapped harder after Nani guessed a crow?
qa.a: She was excited and a bit frustrated that Nani didn't guess right, and wanted everyone to see what she saw.

qa.q: What could Nani do when a child's mime is hard to guess?
qa.a: She could keep guessing and ask simple questions, as she did, until Aditi found the word.

qa.q: How does Kavitha see Aditi's miming?
qa.a: Kavitha sees it as playful and imaginative, and enjoys how it helped everyone find the peacock.

grounding: An older sister observes a preschooler miming tea, driving and a bird to play and to explain what she saw.

passage:
Monday: Aditi was new in the class and hadn't said a word. At snack time she lifted an empty hand to her mouth and tipped it. Karthik Sir guessed, “Water?” She nodded, and he filled her cup.
Wednesday: She mimed a bird flying and pointed at the window. Sir guessed, “You want to see the birds?” She nodded again, but looked disappointed when he didn't take her outside.
Friday: She mimed drinking and whispered, “Water.” Sir smiled wide. “Here you go, Aditi.”

qa.q: What did Aditi mime at snack time on Monday?
qa.a: She lifted an empty hand to her mouth and tipped it.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling on Wednesday when Sir didn't take her outside?
qa.a: She felt disappointed, because she wanted him to understand her mime and act on it. Being shy, she was still expecting adults to guess her meaning.

qa.q: What could Karthik Sir try next to help Aditi use words?
qa.a: He could guess, then say the word slowly and wait a moment, giving Aditi space to repeat it.

qa.q: How might Karthik Sir feel when Aditi whispers “Water” on Friday?
qa.a: He is probably pleased and proud of her, which shows in his wide smile. 😊

grounding: Over a week, a shy new preschooler uses mime to communicate, then begins to add words.

passage:
The wedding hall was so noisy that nobody could hear Mridul. He tugged Keerthana Athai's sari and tipped an invisible cup to his mouth.

"Juice?" she guessed. He shook his head and did it again, slower.

"Water!" He nodded.

When she came back, he gripped an invisible steering wheel and turned it, then pointed at the door.

"You want to go home?" He nodded, then hid his face in her sari.

"Shall we tell Amma together?" she asked. He took her hand.

qa.q: What did Mridul tug to get Keerthana Athai's attention?
qa.a: Keerthana Athai's sari.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when he hid his face in her sari?
qa.a: He was probably tired and shy, maybe overwhelmed by the noisy hall, and embarrassed about asking to go home. He relied on mime and on her guessing because he felt too shy to push further.

qa.q: How did Keerthana Athai help Mridul when words failed?
qa.a: She kept guessing his mimes, checked with him each time, and offered to tell Amma together so he didn't have to speak up alone.

qa.q: What would change if the hall were quiet?
qa.a: Mridul might still mime because he is shy, but he could have been heard more easily if he tried to speak.

grounding: It shows a preschooler miming drinking and driving to explain himself in a noisy hall and a shy child relying on an adult to guess.
